target: AG1’s claim that AI improves everyday life, health, education/work outcomes, accessibility, and workplace safety enough to be good for society.
objection: AI can automate or displace tasks, shift bargaining power toward firms, suppress wages, undermine independent reasoning, repeat racial bias, and create privacy risks; these harms can outweigh the convenience, health, education, inclusion, and safety benefits.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms are unavoidable properties of the technology.
objection: The harms cited—bias, privacy risks, labor disruption, and critical-thinking degradation—primarily come from specific deployment choices such as biased training, weak privacy safeguards, and lack of support, so they are not inherent to AI and can be reduced through responsible deployment.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking for students and adults.
objection: AI used in education and decision-support can provide explanations, guided practice, and prompts that require users to evaluate and refine outputs, so it can support and improve independent reasoning rather than weaken it.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms economic well-being by displacing work and reducing opportunity.
objection: AI can increase productivity, create new tasks or roles alongside automation, and expand overall economic activity, so it can improve economic well-being instead of only harming it.

target: AG2’s broader conclusion that the negative effects of AI dominate the overall societal picture.
objection: If AI can improve critical thinking and economic opportunity, then the cited harms do not establish that AI is overall bad for society.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is socially bad despite its benefits to disabled people and workplace safety.
objection: AI can meaningfully increase accessibility for people with disabilities and reduce workplace injury and danger, and these social inclusion and safety gains are major contributors to societal well-being.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be made good for society by adding contestability and transparency safeguards.
objection: Contestability does not prevent privacy harms from data collection and inference, because surveillance, profiling, and downstream misuse can occur outside any single decision a person can contest and cannot be reliably undone after data has been used or propagated.

target: AG1’s claim that contestability and appeal rights also address racial-bias harms.
objection: Even if a person can contest one AI output, biased training data, measurement, and feedback can keep producing discriminatory outcomes for other people and over time, so systemic racial bias persists beyond any individual appeal.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy and racial-bias risks are preventable enough that AI can be good overall with safeguards.
objection: Because privacy harms and racial discrimination can persist even when some outputs are contestable, contestability alone is insufficient to make AI societally good.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy harms are an unavoidable part of AI.
objection: Privacy harms mainly arise when AI is deployed with weak data governance, and privacy-preserving design choices such as data minimization, purpose limitation, access controls, encryption, and privacy-preserving learning can substantially prevent or reduce those harms.

target: AG2’s claim that racial discrimination is an inevitable downstream result of AI.
objection: Biased outputs can be reduced over time through representative data collection, fairness-aware training, and continuous bias audits and remediation, so persistent racial-bias harms are not inevitable.

target: AG2’s conclusion that AI cannot be good for society even with safeguards.
objection: If AI’s key risks to privacy and racial discrimination can be substantially reduced while its benefits remain available, then AI can still be good for society overall.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving and bias-mitigation safeguards are a realistic general solution.
objection: In real-world AI deployment, competitive pressure to ship quickly, maximize performance, and monetize data often leads to extensive data collection and weak privacy governance, so the needed privacy-preserving practices are not reliably in place.

target: AG1’s claim that ongoing bias audits and remediation can usually control discrimination.
objection: Effective bias-aware practices require sustained resources, transparency, accountability, and continuous model governance, and these are often under-resourced in rapid, profit-driven deployments, making consistent remediation unreliable.

target: AG1’s assumption that safeguards will usually keep AI harms under control in practice.
objection: When privacy governance and continuous bias remediation are not reliably implemented, surveillance/profiling, misuse, and discriminatory outcomes remain active and disproportionately burden people with fewer institutional resources to resist or detect harm.

target: AG1’s claim that theoretical benefits with safeguards are enough to justify AI as good for society.
objection: If privacy and racial-equity harms persist widely in typical deployments, then AI cannot be considered good for society overall, even if it might be beneficial under ideal governance conditions.
